title: Malintzin (Doña Marina)
summary: Malintzin, called Doña Marina by the Spanish, was a Nahua woman who served as interpreter and adviser to Hernán Cortés after being given to him in Tabasco in 1519. Sources disagree on her birthplace and on how to judge her role: some call her a traitor, others a survivor with little power or a founder of Mexican culture.

uncertainty.note: Only one opened source gives birth and death years, both approximate. No source gives exact dates.

where.modern_name: Tabasco, Mexico (where she was given to Cortés in 1519)
where.historical_name: Tabasco, territory of a Maya cacique, at the time she was given to Cortés

importance.justification: Britain Untold says she translated for and advised Cortés and helped secure the Tlaxcalan alliance; JSTOR Daily and Tennessee State describe her as a key and much-debated figure.

sources.title: Malintzin: The Translator Who Changed the Course of History

reviewer_note: She left no writings, so all accounts are secondhand. Origins differ: Britain Untold says the Coatzacoalcos region; Tennessee State gives no birthplace. The pin is Tabasco, where Britain Untold and JSTOR Daily say she was given to Cortés, not her birthplace. Perspectives vary across sources: traitor (Mexican tradition, per Britain Untold and Tennessee State), survivor or agent, and symbol of mestizaje.
